source_quality.notes: All 32 page texts, four full-paper contact sheets, four detail sheets, and key original-resolution formula/code pages were reviewed; official 2019 Problem A was also read in full.

task_reconstruction.objective: Estimate dragon growth, energy expenditure and intake, ecological effects, climate-dependent resource needs, community support under varying assistance, story guidance, and a real-world transfer.
inputs: official hatch and one-year biological anchors plus fictional dragon traits
flying-animal metabolism, bone strength, food energy, trophic rates, and ecosystem productivity
ranked patch-occupancy parameters, three climate scenarios, region areas, and human restoration controls
outputs: monthly mass, expenditure, intake, and body-size bound
forest, desert, and ice support area plus population occupancy trajectories
intervention sensitivity, ecological laws, a two-page letter, community-size analysis, and real-world application
task_reconstruction.decision: Translate biological and ecological estimates into climate-aware story and management guidance while preserving entity level, time basis, and model coupling.

contributions.summary: Names and decodes a two-layer architecture: one dragon energy-growth model coupled to n native occupancy states.
Separates rest and action metabolic calibrations using flying-animal data.
Combines a bone-strength upper bound with a calibrated VB mass trajectory.
Maps resource area into a time-varying habitat-loss forcing for a Tilman occupancy model.
Adds repair strength and lag as an explicit feedback term.
Uses a common simulation and visual template for forest, desert, and ice sheet.
Discloses calibration arrays, k search, ODE loops, plotting structure, and embedded constants.

edges.handoff: State-specific expenditure coefficients enter the net food-energy budget.
The net usable energy fraction K supplies the dynamic mass budget.
The bone-strength mass bound fixes M_inf for the VB trajectory.
The fitted mass path is substituted for the unsolved energy-growth state.
Rest/action allometry supplies the maintenance term in the growth balance.
Required ingestion energy supplies the numerator of minimum support area.
The age-mass trajectory drives age-varying resource demand.
Minimum support area s(t) is multiplied into dragon activity scope S(t).
The base ranked occupancy system receives the dragon damage forcing.
Unrepaired damage D1 is the delayed input to human restoration.
Restored occupancy trajectories feed eta and xi metrics.
Unassisted occupancy trajectories provide the comparison baseline.
The ranked base dynamics are used to claim an equilibrium recursion.
Dragon damage D1 enters the claimed extinction threshold.
Regression code implements the state-specific allometric calibration.
Weight code implements k search and the VB curve.
Population code attempts to implement delayed restoration scenarios.

assumptions.summary: Dragon biology and behavior transfer from warm-blooded animals.
Rare large climate shocks are excluded over the modeled horizon.
Every initial ecosystem begins at homeostasis.
Dragon body function is invariant over a long life.
Dragons have the strongest competitive ability and few natural enemies.
Injury does not change body function.
Gravity and structure impose an upper mass.
Bird and bat rate scaling applies to dragons.
Most fire energy scales with the mass of food roasted.
Bulk density and bone-to-body geometry do not change with size.
Every modeled population has the same d.
Dragon living scope is five times minimum support area.
Human repair equals mu times past dragon damage after a fixed lag.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Nineteen energy, growth, occupancy, and restoration symbols establish the intended interfaces.
Four flying-animal rows preview rest and action mass-specific rates.
Twelve rows provide the appendix calibration source, with unexplained regression exclusions.
Production, respiration, and assimilation ranges parameterize trophic transfer.
Three compressive-strength values motivate the selected dragon-bone stress.
Forest, desert, and ice-sheet productivity ranges and averages drive area scenarios.
NPP, rest fraction, population count, q, and d differ by climate.
The official 10 kg hatch mass and 30-40 kg one-year range calibrate k.
12.9 t and 79.2 t states are selected from the VB trajectory without named ages.
Three S0 values per climate define the ecosystem comparison grid.
mu in {0,0.4,0.8} and lag in {12,600} define intervention comparisons.
Kleiber, VB, Hanski, and Tilman references support model-family choices.
Wikipedia pages provide qualitative biome descriptions but not quantitative parameter calibration.
The printed driver fixes an ice-sheet-like 15-population scenario.
The code embeds 5.35e5, 33930, and 0.5655 without a unit ledger.
The source task requires varying-assistance community size and a concrete real-world application.

The 12.9 t and 79.2 t values match approximately 300 and 1000 months.
Appendix constants reproduce about 5.93e6 m2 for the adult forest scope.
Three region sizes hold other forest parameters fixed.
Three region sizes hold other desert parameters fixed.
Three region sizes hold other ice parameters fixed.
Figures 14-16 compare no repair, mu=0.4, and mu=0.8 at a common lag.

writing_logic.summary: Motivation -> 1+n architecture -> growth -> occupancy -> three climates -> results -> sensitivity -> limitations.
Story traits -> ecological significance -> model-family literature -> joint gap -> contribution -> roadmap.
Expenditure -> fire/intake -> assimilation -> mass allocation -> physical bound -> VB path.
Mass and energy -> NPP support area -> activity scope -> destroyed habitat -> occupancy response.
Shared metrics and plot grammar support within-biome area sweeps and cross-biome comparison.
Simulation trajectories -> equilibrium condition -> extinction threshold -> parity claim.
Growth -> physical bound -> food -> area -> ecological risk -> story recommendation.

language_observations.summary: Reusable move: fiction-to-real ecology motivation; order fictional premise -> ecological game -> real-world reference; boundary: Motivation must name the analytical transfer, not merely call the topic interesting.
Reusable move: named two-layer model architecture; order one growth layer -> n ecosystem populations -> combined purpose; boundary: A coined architecture must immediately decode every component.
Reusable move: mechanism-to-growth capsule; order Kleiber expenditure -> food-chain intake -> mass trajectory; boundary: A method capsule should terminate in an output rather than a list of tools.
Reusable move: base-model modification capsule; order base model -> dragon interference -> population response; boundary: Name what is inherited and what is modified.
Reusable move: parallel environment application; order warm temperate -> arid -> arctic -> common outputs; boundary: Parallel scenarios require common metrics and units.
Reusable move: unit-bearing headline result; order adult state -> energy -> minimum region; boundary: Headline values must preserve subject, time basis, and scenario.
Reusable move: named emergent-law claim; order simulation pattern -> named law -> ecological interpretation; boundary: A named law needs an explicit condition and distinct cases.
Reusable move: validation-and-limit close; order sensitivity factors -> strengths -> weaknesses; boundary: The close should distinguish sensitivity from validation.
Reusable move: source-trait context; order story premise -> ordinary biology -> special abilities; boundary: Fictional traits should be separated into accepted givens and modeled consequences.
Reusable move: dual-use significance; order story consistency -> ecological insight -> research objective; boundary: Significance should not imply empirical validation that is not performed.
Reusable move: literature ladder to gap; order population growth -> predator-prey -> metapopulation -> missing joint factors; boundary: A gap paragraph should compare capabilities on the same axis.
Reusable move: gap-to-contribution pivot; order identified gap -> combined model -> target outputs; boundary: The contribution claim should preview the coupling interface.
Reusable move: section-by-section roadmap; order assumptions -> growth -> ecosystem -> implementation -> results -> evaluation; boundary: A roadmap should mirror the body order exactly.
Reusable move: analogue permission with rationale; order assumption -> reason -> enabled inference; boundary: An analogue assumption must state which traits transfer and which do not.
Reusable move: stable-environment boundary; order time horizon -> excluded shocks -> homeostatic baseline; boundary: Stability boundaries need a time scale and excluded disturbance classes.
Reusable move: long-life functional invariance; order longevity -> fixed physiology -> growth simplification; boundary: Age invariance should not silently remove senescence or reproduction.

Reusable move: dominance and trauma boundary; order competitive rank -> few enemies -> fixed function after injury; boundary: Dominance is not equivalent to habitat destruction and needs an operational link.
Reusable move: finite-size premise; order gravity -> biological structure -> finite mass; boundary: A bound assumption should be followed by an independently defined constraint.
Reusable move: typed notation registry; order energy states -> mass/rates -> ecology states -> human controls; boundary: Notation must preserve dimensions and avoid reusing symbols across models.
Reusable move: energy-state partition; order intake -> assimilation -> expenditure -> growth absorption -> fire; boundary: Every energy stock or flow needs a consistent time basis.
Reusable move: state-control notation split; order state p_i -> migration c_i -> death d_i -> lag -> human impact; boundary: State, rate, ratio, and delay symbols need distinct units.
Reusable move: model workflow preview; order expenditure -> food-chain transfer -> absorbed growth -> size limit; boundary: A workflow preview should match the subsequent equation order.
Reusable move: diagram-led conservation interface; order solar input -> trophic transfer -> partition -> body-size limit; boundary: A diagram equation and body equation must use the same terms.
Reusable move: factor decomposition; order mass condition -> motion state -> fire exception; boundary: A factor decomposition should state whether terms are additive or conditional.
Reusable move: empirical law introduction; order qualitative size effect -> power law -> parameter definition; boundary: A cited law must distinguish total rate from per-mass rate.

Reusable move: state classification before calibration; order state definitions -> analogue data -> state constants; boundary: State classes require either proportions or scenarios before aggregation.
Reusable move: log-linear calibration handoff; order normalize by mass -> log transform -> linear fit -> q0; boundary: If a theoretical slope is imposed, distinguish it from a freely fitted slope.
Reusable move: data-table-to-fit pairing; order sample rows -> complete appendix -> fit lines -> constants; boundary: A sample/full-data split should disclose exclusions and fitted coefficients.

Reusable move: fictional mechanism anchored in physical analogy; order gland -> flammable liquid -> ignition -> energy estimate; boundary: A mechanism narrative does not replace a sourced energy calculation.
Reusable move: trophic-class intake framing; order food web -> trophic classes -> losses -> assimilation rate; boundary: Trophic efficiency and individual digestion efficiency must not be conflated.

Reusable move: energy-budget closure; order assimilated input -> growth absorption -> motion expenditure -> fire; boundary: Every energy term must appear consistently in the diagram, prose, and equations.
Reusable move: energy-to-mass differential handoff; order net usable intake -> maintenance -> growth energy -> mass rate; boundary: The energy-per-mass coefficient must be defined and dimensioned.
Reusable move: physical constraint pivot; order growth model -> gravity -> bone support -> mass bound; boundary: A physical bound should identify its governing failure mode.
Reusable move: material-data transfer; order reference bones -> chosen safety uplift -> dragon strength; boundary: A selected material value needs a transparent aggregation rule.

Reusable move: geometric safety-factor derivation; order stress capacity -> weight -> geometry -> safety factor -> mass upper bound; boundary: Density and geometry units must close before reporting the mass bound.
Reusable move: model-family selection; order variable growth rate -> VB ODE -> integrated solution; boundary: A growth-family choice should be linked to the modeled organism and horizon.
Reusable move: three-anchor parameter calibration; order initial mass -> one-year mass -> asymptote -> k; boundary: Calibration should report residuals and the selected value beyond four digits.
Reusable move: curve-plus-rate encoding; order time-mass curve -> color rate -> fast-growth age band; boundary: A dual encoding needs an explicit colorbar unit and reproducible peak calculation.
Reusable move: individual-to-ecosystem scale handoff; order dragon state -> given region -> population response; boundary: The handoff must specify which dragon outputs enter the ecosystem model.

Reusable move: resource-area causal chain; order solar energy -> producer biomass -> consumer transfer -> dragon intake -> area; boundary: Each conversion must preserve mass/energy and annual/monthly time bases.
Reusable move: cross-biome productivity comparison; order ecosystem type -> range -> average -> area implication; boundary: Use the same productivity unit and trophic conversion for every scenario.
Reusable move: minimum-area interface; order NPP density -> area -> net assimilation -> intake; boundary: The named energy conversion cannot disappear from the displayed interface.

Reusable move: base-model conceptual setup; order fragmented habitats -> metapopulation -> competition -> occupancy; boundary: A base model description should define what a patch and occupancy mean operationally.
Reusable move: ranked competition dynamics; order colonization -> free habitat -> death -> displacement; boundary: Printed and coded competition coefficients must agree.

Reusable move: ranked geometric parameter initialization; order equal death -> initial occupancy -> migration hierarchy; boundary: Initialization formulas need parameter admissibility and normalization checks.

Reusable move: introduced-species-as-interference framing; order homeostasis -> new species -> habitat competition -> magnification; boundary: Interference should be defined as a measurable state or forcing term.

Reusable move: resource area to destroyed-habitat forcing; order minimum food area -> activity multiplier -> region area -> destroyed ratio -> ODE forcing; boundary: The activity-scope multiplier requires evidence or sensitivity.

Reusable move: delayed restoration feedback; order damage history -> lag -> repair fraction -> restored habitat -> population response; boundary: A delayed feedback model is not an ordinary ODE and needs history data.
Reusable move: long-horizon simulation rationale; order slow succession -> nonlinear system -> numerical simulation; boundary: Simulation is justified by model structure, not by horizon alone.

Reusable move: solver selection statement; order equation system -> solver family -> scenario runs -> appendix code; boundary: A solver statement should include tolerances, delay handling, and reproducible code.
Reusable move: body-to-code handoff; order regression -> weight -> population -> space-energy; boundary: Appendix routing should name which script produces each result.
Reusable move: nested competition update; order sum occupancy -> rank interactions -> delay branch -> ode45; boundary: Published code must be executable without ellipsis placeholders.
Reusable move: paired impact metrics; order occupancy amount -> surviving types -> normalization -> interpretation; boundary: Metric names must distinguish remaining ratios from reductions.
Reusable move: scenario-selection rationale; order migration premise -> warm temperate -> arid -> arctic; boundary: Scenario narratives should connect to parameter changes.
Reusable move: compact scenario parameter ledger; order NPP -> rest fraction -> population count -> q -> death; boundary: Every header must match a defined symbol and unit.
Reusable move: full calibration data disclosure; order species -> mass -> rest rate -> action rate; boundary: Full data should reconcile with all regression inputs and exclusions.

Reusable move: log-transform implementation; order input arrays -> log transform -> free slope/intercept -> plot; boundary: Code-derived coefficients should be reported rather than replaced by theoretical labels.
Reusable move: three-panel result narration; order area curve -> intake curve -> expenditure curve -> cross-biome order; boundary: Panel narration must identify left, middle, and right correctly.
Reusable move: young-versus-adult comparison; order life stage -> mass -> monthly energy -> minimum area; boundary: A stage label needs a corresponding age and activity schedule.
Reusable move: single-to-group scaling; order single adult area -> three dragons -> football-field analogy; boundary: Group scaling must state whether dragon ages and overlap are identical.

Reusable move: paired trajectory-and-index reading; order population trajectories -> extinction criterion -> aggregate occupancy; boundary: The population-type statistic should be computed consistently with its caption.
Reusable move: within-biome area sweep; order small region -> medium region -> large region -> extinction response; boundary: Area sensitivity should vary one factor with all others fixed.
Reusable move: cross-biome analogy plus exception; order larger resource need -> rank exchange -> area response; boundary: A qualitative anomaly should be tied to a state equation or diagnostic.

Reusable move: collapse-to-survival contrast; order small region collapse -> intermediate survival -> large region survival; boundary: Do not call a ratio of surviving types an occupancy reduction ratio.
Reusable move: stability-timescale contrast; order resource scarcity -> collapse risk -> relaxation time; boundary: Stability, recovery, and extinction need separate definitions.
Reusable move: intervention sensitivity setup; order baseline forest -> repair strength -> lag -> population metrics; boundary: A delay sweep must specify the history and solver treatment.
Reusable move: baseline-to-stronger-repair comparison; order no repair -> mu=0.4 -> mu=0.8 -> surviving types; boundary: State the same evaluation horizon and region area for every comparison.

Reusable move: timeliness comparison; order same repair fraction -> short lag -> long lag -> trajectory recovery; boundary: A claim about speed should use a recovery-time metric, not only endpoint survival.
Reusable move: monotone policy summary; order small help -> greater repair -> shorter lag -> endangered populations; boundary: Monotonic language must be supported over the sampled parameter range.
Reusable move: model-to-action translation; order monitor -> reintroduce -> restore habitat -> provide food; boundary: Recommendations should map to explicit model controls or measured states.

Reusable move: simulation-to-law transition; order complex dynamics -> observed patterns -> named laws; boundary: An observed pattern needs a derivation or falsifiable criterion before being called a law.

Reusable move: piecewise equilibrium statement; order equilibrium condition -> positive occupancy -> zero truncation; boundary: Every new equilibrium symbol must be defined and derived from the base ODE.
Reusable move: threshold condition; order destroyed ratio -> death-to-colonization ratio -> top-i extinction; boundary: A threshold should be checked against simulation and symbol definitions.
Reusable move: case-based structural claim; order extinction parity -> surviving rank parity -> long-run strength; boundary: Odd and even cases must be separately stated and evidenced.

Reusable move: result-to-policy bridge; order simulation finding -> policy category -> implementation measure; boundary: A bridge should make clear which recommendations are model-derived and which are domain additions.
Reusable move: state-observation extension; order state p_i -> field observation -> update schedule; boundary: Monitoring requires a mapping from observations to occupancy estimates.

Reusable move: extinction-response extension; order detected extinction -> reintroduction -> competition response; boundary: Reintroduction changes the state dimension and cannot be represented only by mu.

Reusable move: predation-pressure extension; order assistance level -> reduced wild predation -> human resources; boundary: Provisioning must connect to the official varying-assistance community calculation.
Reusable move: evidence-triangulation claim; order real analogue -> fiction anchor -> dragon parameter; boundary: Triangulation requires a reconciliation rule when sources disagree.

Reusable move: scope-and-transfer inventory; order interaction coverage -> long horizon -> adjustable environments; boundary: Transferability depends on parameter identifiability, not adjustability alone.

Reusable move: computational-and-seasonal limitations; order large state dimension -> seasonal omission; boundary: Limitations should include coupling, calibration, and validation gaps as well as compute cost.
Reusable move: architecture restatement; order growth layer -> ecosystem layer -> combined purpose; boundary: A conclusion should restate the coupling result, not only model names.
Reusable move: method-result recap; order energy -> area -> population influence -> ecological response; boundary: Recap values should preserve the final model version and scenario.
Reusable move: intervention-and-action close; order human effect -> reconstruction -> measures; boundary: The close should disclose unmodeled official outputs.
Reusable move: audience-aligned model introduction; order audience relationship -> two model names -> story-use promise; boundary: Audience alignment should simplify without altering model claims.
Reusable move: life-course narrative; order changing rate -> puberty band -> adult slowdown; boundary: A narrative age band should be traceable to the derivative calculation.
Reusable move: analogy-backed headline; order gravity constraint -> upper mass -> elephant analogy; boundary: A comparison should not obscure the assumptions behind the bound.
Reusable move: stakeholder-scale resource result; order energy intake -> prey count -> young/adult area -> three-dragon area; boundary: Prey counts need a time basis and mass/energy conversion.

Reusable move: risk explanation in plain language; order introduced species -> no enemies -> habitat damage -> extinction risk; boundary: Plain language must preserve the modeled mechanism rather than overstate causality.

Reusable move: scenario-to-story recommendation; order ice-sheet struggle -> larger region -> reduced proportional damage -> story choice; boundary: A wider range is not equivalent to lower total ecological impact.
Reusable move: foundational-source ladder; order growth -> allometry -> metapopulation -> biodiversity; boundary: References should support the exact equation or parameter attributed to them.
Reusable move: scenario-and-policy source tail; order biome definitions -> conservation actions; boundary: General encyclopedia pages should not substitute for quantitative parameter provenance.

Reusable move: regression-code disclosure; order arrays -> polyfit -> plot -> display coefficients; boundary: Displayed coefficients should match the actual free regression.

Reusable move: equation-to-loop translation; order occupancy sum -> ranked competition -> delay branch -> derivative; boundary: Code notation must match the printed equation indices.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A named architecture and unit-bearing result ladder improve first-pass navigability, but headline values must distinguish expenditure, intake, and climate.
A full causal diagram helps a judge trace coupling, provided its conservation equation matches the body.
Parallel scenario plots make climate comparison fast, but axes, entity level, and minimum-versus-scope semantics must be explicit.
Audience-specific compression is useful only when it carries corrected final model versions and all required outputs.

weaknesses.summary: The Abstract reports an upper mass of 1.17e3 kg, while Equation 13, the letter, and Appendix C use about 1.17e5 or 1.2e5 kg; the summary is low by a factor of 100.

The Abstract calls 2.4e11 J/month adult energy intake, but at the 79.2 t state the appendix formula gives about 2.40e11 J/month expenditure and about 4.27e11 J/month gross intake after growth and K=0.5655.
The Abstract presents 1.8e7 m2 as a general minimum region for three dragons, but the value is the temperate-forest activity scope; the same code gives much larger desert and ice-sheet requirements.

The introduction claims the work provides insight into realistic ecological games, but no specific non-dragon real-world application, data case, or external validation is described as required by the official task.
Table 1 assigns q the unit J/(kg h), although Equation 1 uses q as whole-animal metabolic rate and Equation 2 separately defines the mass-specific rate q_hat.
The symbol q is reused in Section 4.2 as a geometric occupancy parameter after serving as metabolic rate in Section 3; the cross-model notation collision is not acknowledged.
Table 1 labels c_i without a unit even though it is a migration rate used with d_i in month^-1 dynamics.
Equation 8 introduces lambda without defining its unit or value; Appendix E silently sets it to 2e7, the same number used for food energy per kilogram.
Figure 1 states E_in AR = E_assimilate = E_expend + E_absorb and omits E_fire, while Equation 5 and the code treat fire as a separate energy term.
The symbol table defines M in kilograms, but the q0 regression is fitted with mass in grams; the displayed equations do not expose the required 1000^(3/4) conversion.
The plotted rest and action lines are printed with fixed slope -0.25, while Appendix B freely fits both slope and intercept; direct regression gives slopes about -0.2692 and -0.2645.
The 3 g hummingbird row appears in Appendix Table 7 but is excluded from both regression arrays without explanation.
Appendix B names the action fit handle rest_line and the rest fit handle action_line; the final legend happens to look correct, but the implementation names obscure the state mapping.
The action state combines flying, hunting, and other activity under one coefficient and no time schedule; the model cannot separately answer the official flight-energy question.
The fire coefficient 6.69e6 J/kg is described as an estimate but has no heat-capacity calculation, temperature target, efficiency, source, or uncertainty.
The proposed gland, flammable liquid, and electric-eel ignition mechanism is speculative narrative and is not connected to the reported fire-energy coefficient.
Table 3 mixes biological production, respiration, and individual assimilation percentages without a consistent trophic energy ledger.
K=0.5655 assumes every kilogram of food is roasted with the same fire cost and that fire energy scales exactly with ingested mass.
The paper writes an energy-driven mass ODE in Equation 8 but never solves it jointly; Section 3.4 switches to an independently calibrated VB growth curve.
The dragon density is printed as 1e3 kg/m2 rather than kg/m3, making Equations 10-13 dimensionally invalid as written.
Bone strength is set 20-69 percent above the three table values with no aggregation or biological transfer rationale.
The geometric relation cube_root(V)=10 sqrt(A) is asserted without anatomical evidence and effectively fixes a constant body-to-bone slenderness across all sizes.
The factor-25 daily-activity load condition has no derivation, citation, or sensitivity analysis.
The body-size bound considers only axial bone compression and omits buckling, bending, fatigue, flight loading, muscle power, heat dissipation, and circulation.
Reference [7] is titled that the VB equation should not be used to model age and size at maturity, yet the paper uses it without discussing that limitation.
Only hatch and one-year masses calibrate k after M_inf is fixed; no later narrative size observations, residuals, or alternate growth-family comparison are used.
The stated fastest-growth band of 30-80 years is broad; the retained formula has a single derivative maximum near 527 months or 43.9 years, but that calculation is not shown.
Figure 3's colorbar encodes growth rate without a labeled unit, and its values are not tied to the claimed 30-80 year band.
Using Table 3's own ranges, primary-consumer NAR=(1-respiration)AR is about 0.28-0.40, not the asserted approximately 20 percent.
Equation 16 equates energy to NPP mass density times area and NAR, omitting the stated 1.8e7 J/kg conversion, grams-to-kilograms conversion, and years-to-months conversion.
Section 4.1 first says s supports three dragons, Section 4.3 calls s a dragon's minimum area, and Appendix E applies an additional factor of three; the entity level is inconsistent.
Appendix E hides multiple physical conversions inside the unexplained constant 33930, so the displayed Equation 16 is not the implemented interface.
NPP is described as consumer mass although net primary productivity is producer biomass; trophic roles are mislabeled at the model boundary.
Equation 17 prints c_i in the displacement sum, while Appendix D uses c(j); the governing equation and code implement different competitive interactions.
Initial occupied area is treated as competitive strength without ecological justification, so rank is inferred from the state it later predicts.
The geometric initial occupancies and migration rates are not checked for total occupancy, parameter admissibility, or empirical fit.
The activity scope S=5s is unsupported and is never varied even though it drives every ecosystem impact result.
The model equates the entire dragon activity scope with destroyed habitat, rather than representing predation, fire, water use, waste, competition, or partial habitat use.
Three dragons are represented by multiplying area rather than modeling overlapping territories, different ages, or separate movement paths.
D2 is called a destroyed-habitat ratio, but Equation 22 adds it back as repaired habitat; the symbol's stated meaning and algebraic role have opposite directions.
Equation 22 is described as a first-order linear differential system, but products p_i p_j make it nonlinear and S(t) makes it nonautonomous.
The repair fraction and lag have no empirical source, cost, labor requirement, capacity bound, or connection to community size.
eta is named a reduction ratio but equals remaining total occupancy divided by baseline; larger eta means less reduction.
xi is also named a reduction ratio but equals the fraction of population types that remain.
Appendix D counts states below 1e-4 and outputs count/max_i, which is an extinction fraction, the complement of the xi reported in figure captions.
The extinction threshold p_i<1e-4 appears only in code and is not justified or tested for sensitivity.
Table 6 labels the population-count column i even though its values 60, 30, and 15 represent n; units and sources for the parameter ledger are absent.
The 12.9 t and 79.2 t result states correspond to about 300 and 1000 months under the VB curve, but the text calls them young and adult without giving ages.
At the 79.2 t state, intake is about 1.78 times expenditure under K=0.5655, not only slightly larger as claimed.
The reported 5.9e6 m2 forest value is the paper's S=5s activity scope, not the minimum food-support area s, yet it is described as the minimum region.
The highlighted 1.8e7 m2 three-dragon value applies to the temperate forest only; the same appendix formulas give about 3.24e8 m2 in desert and 1.50e10 m2 on ice.
The text says desert area is ten times the forest value, but its own NPP and rest-fraction parameters imply about 18.2 times for the adult state.
The three-panel description calls both the first and third panels the left one; the third panel is energy expenditure.
Captions report xi at 12,000 months, while the body sometimes calls the right-hand eta curve the reduction ratio of population types, mixing the two metrics.
The claim that dominant populations are more affected than vulnerable populations is observed from selected trajectories but not derived from the model or tested across parameters.
The desert discussion calls the first 2,000 units years, but all equations and plot axes use months.
The ice-sheet discussion says eta of population types is zero; population-type survival is xi, while eta measures total occupancy.
Equation 23 replaces the death symbol d_i with undefined m_i and does not reconcile its summation with Equation 17.
D1>=1-m_i/c_i ignores the equilibrium occupancy terms that also determine extinction, so it is not the general exact threshold claimed.
The Odd-even Symmetry Law repeats the same odd-extinction/even-rank sentence twice and never states the even-extinction case.
The Odd-even claim cites an empty 'Figure .' reference and has no dedicated figure, derivation, table, or counterexample test.
The prose says Figure 15 is the no-reconstruction baseline, but the baseline is Figure 14; Figure 15 already uses mu=0.4.
Figure 17 with a 600-month lag shows strong oscillations and eta falling near 0.45 before partial recovery, yet the analysis reports only the endpoint and calls recovery faster or better.
Monitoring, reintroduction, soil repair, and feeding recommendations are not mapped to separate controls or costs; all are rhetorically compressed into mu.
The official requirement for community size under varying assistance is not answered: no assistance-level parameter maps feeding, labor, population, or infrastructure to dragon needs.
The strengths claim real-world transferability because parameters are adjustable, but no parameter identification or external case demonstrates transfer.
The limitations list only computational scale and seasonality, omitting the paper's major dimensional, calibration, coupling, and reproducibility gaps.
The letter says an adult dragon must eat 480 sheep weighing 25 kg but gives no time basis; 480 sheep provide 2.4e11 J gross, which is only the reported expenditure, not required gross intake.
Using the paper's own K and adult growth state requires about 21,347 kg or 854 25-kg sheep per month, not 480, before uncertainty in prey energy or waste.
The letter presents the 1.8e7 m2 forest result as a universal three-dragon minimum and omits the much larger desert and ice-sheet results.
The letter claims a wider dragon activity range causes less ecological damage; the model only reduces proportional damage D1=S/S0 when total region S0 grows, not total disturbed area.
The letter gives no community-size result, assistance-level comparison, quantified restoration cost, or warm-temperate/arid/arctic resource table.
In weightFigure.m the function handles m_t and dm_dt are printed as commented lines, but the script later calls them; the published code cannot run as shown.
evalPopulationChange.m prints func_d=@(t)... as a literal placeholder, so the population figures cannot be reproduced from the appendix.
The printed population driver fixes max_i=15, pp=0.003, alpha_r=0.3, and q=0.3, covering only the ice-sheet example rather than all forest, desert, and restoration figures.
calcDragonSpaceAndEnergy.m prints every func_d and energy function handle as @(t)... placeholders, so Figure 4 is not reproducible from the published code.

independent_extensions.summary: Separate BMR, flight, hunting, fire, thermoregulation, growth, and reproduction energy with calibrated activity schedules.
Rebuild the NPP-to-area ledger with explicit producer biomass, trophic efficiencies, energy density, time conversion, incumbent demand, and sustainable harvest.
Calibrate patch-occupancy states and rates from a real ecosystem, then add direct predation and fire disturbance rather than treating all scope as destroyed.
Replace the fivefold scope assumption with a movement/home-range model and overlapping territories for three age-specific dragons.
Model restoration as constrained controls with costs, capacity, monitoring, reintroduction, and habitat recovery dynamics.
Compute community labor, food supply, land, logistics, and infrastructure across explicit assistance levels from zero to full provisioning.
Add climate pathways through water, thermoregulation, migration, seasonal NPP, prey availability, and shelter, then feed them back to area and community outputs.
Publish executable code, named unit conversions, complete scenario files, solver tolerances, residuals, and a result ledger.
Test the extinction threshold and parity claim over parameter grids with counterexample search and correct surviving/extinct metrics.
Apply the corrected coupled model to a concrete invasive-predator or rewilding case with observed data and domain-specific limits.

unresolved_questions.summary: The Abstract reports an upper mass of 1.17e3 kg, while Equation 13, the letter, and Appendix C use about 1.17e5 or 1.2e5 kg; the summary is low by a factor of 100.

The Abstract calls 2.4e11 J/month adult energy intake, but at the 79.2 t state the appendix formula gives about 2.40e11 J/month expenditure and about 4.27e11 J/month gross intake after growth and K=0.5655.
The Abstract presents 1.8e7 m2 as a general minimum region for three dragons, but the value is the temperate-forest activity scope; the same code gives much larger desert and ice-sheet requirements.

The introduction claims the work provides insight into realistic ecological games, but no specific non-dragon real-world application, data case, or external validation is described as required by the official task.
Table 1 assigns q the unit J/(kg h), although Equation 1 uses q as whole-animal metabolic rate and Equation 2 separately defines the mass-specific rate q_hat.
The symbol q is reused in Section 4.2 as a geometric occupancy parameter after serving as metabolic rate in Section 3; the cross-model notation collision is not acknowledged.
Table 1 labels c_i without a unit even though it is a migration rate used with d_i in month^-1 dynamics.
Equation 8 introduces lambda without defining its unit or value; Appendix E silently sets it to 2e7, the same number used for food energy per kilogram.
Figure 1 states E_in AR = E_assimilate = E_expend + E_absorb and omits E_fire, while Equation 5 and the code treat fire as a separate energy term.
The symbol table defines M in kilograms, but the q0 regression is fitted with mass in grams; the displayed equations do not expose the required 1000^(3/4) conversion.
The plotted rest and action lines are printed with fixed slope -0.25, while Appendix B freely fits both slope and intercept; direct regression gives slopes about -0.2692 and -0.2645.
The 3 g hummingbird row appears in Appendix Table 7 but is excluded from both regression arrays without explanation.
Appendix B names the action fit handle rest_line and the rest fit handle action_line; the final legend happens to look correct, but the implementation names obscure the state mapping.
The action state combines flying, hunting, and other activity under one coefficient and no time schedule; the model cannot separately answer the official flight-energy question.
The fire coefficient 6.69e6 J/kg is described as an estimate but has no heat-capacity calculation, temperature target, efficiency, source, or uncertainty.
The proposed gland, flammable liquid, and electric-eel ignition mechanism is speculative narrative and is not connected to the reported fire-energy coefficient.
Table 3 mixes biological production, respiration, and individual assimilation percentages without a consistent trophic energy ledger.
K=0.5655 assumes every kilogram of food is roasted with the same fire cost and that fire energy scales exactly with ingested mass.
The paper writes an energy-driven mass ODE in Equation 8 but never solves it jointly; Section 3.4 switches to an independently calibrated VB growth curve.
The dragon density is printed as 1e3 kg/m2 rather than kg/m3, making Equations 10-13 dimensionally invalid as written.
Bone strength is set 20-69 percent above the three table values with no aggregation or biological transfer rationale.
The geometric relation cube_root(V)=10 sqrt(A) is asserted without anatomical evidence and effectively fixes a constant body-to-bone slenderness across all sizes.
The factor-25 daily-activity load condition has no derivation, citation, or sensitivity analysis.
The body-size bound considers only axial bone compression and omits buckling, bending, fatigue, flight loading, muscle power, heat dissipation, and circulation.
Reference [7] is titled that the VB equation should not be used to model age and size at maturity, yet the paper uses it without discussing that limitation.
Only hatch and one-year masses calibrate k after M_inf is fixed; no later narrative size observations, residuals, or alternate growth-family comparison are used.
The stated fastest-growth band of 30-80 years is broad; the retained formula has a single derivative maximum near 527 months or 43.9 years, but that calculation is not shown.
Figure 3's colorbar encodes growth rate without a labeled unit, and its values are not tied to the claimed 30-80 year band.
